blocks.clean_summary: Small talk about New York City real estate. Faraaz remarks that even Queens is expensive and that the south side of Harlem is 'extremely gentrified... all highrises now.' Drazen reminisces about ice skating at the Lasker rink at the northern end of Central Park in 1985, when buildings on Central Park North were vacant. Faraaz then abruptly asks Drazen what he thinks of Giuliani.

corrections.basis: Drazen describes 'ice skating at the at the Alaska rink there at the northern end of Central Park' (line 11). The skating rink at the northern end of Central Park is the Lasker Rink; 'Alaska' is a phonetic garble of 'Lasker'.

blocks.clean_summary: Continued small talk. Drazen explains he was not in NYC when Giuliani was mayor; when he lived there, Ed Koch was mayor, and Giuliani became mayor only after Drazen had left the city. He recalls thinking in 1985 that the derelict buildings around Central Park had tremendous potential and wishing he had money to buy them.

corrections.basis: Line 30: 'when I was there, Ed Cotch was mayor' — Ed Koch was NYC mayor 1978-1989, matching Drazen's stated mid-1980s residency and the Giuliani-succession discussion.

blocks.clean_summary: Faraaz describes present-day NYC policing above 112th Street — flood lights every three blocks and roughly eight uniformed officers every second block 'just for presence' — calling it dystopian. He also remarks on empty Chinese-built properties in Long Island City sitting vacant for three years, speculating it is clearly money laundering ('clearly la[under] money... this doesn't make sense'). Drazen agrees he used to wonder how it all keeps going.

corrections.basis: Line 51 context: properties 'built by Chinese... building companies empty for three years now no one's there and I'm like this Clearly, you just clearly la money. This this doesn't make sense.' Vacant-property context supports 'launder money'; moderate confidence, no legal weight.
Line 49; context is neighborhood transformation via police presence and lighting. Insufficient basis to fix a single reading; left unresolved.

blocks.clean_summary: Drazen recounts his biography: in 1985 he had not yet started law school; he graduated from the University of Florida, moved to NYC in December 1984, and notes UF was strict — many students got a letter after their second year saying they were no longer students. Faraaz asks whether Drazen came back to Binghamton in 1985 (he did not).

corrections.basis: Line 61: 'So you came back to Binghamington 1985.' Drazen practices in Binghamton, NY (NDNY/Broome County venue of Rahman v. UHS); phonetic garble.

Line 65, Faraaz interjecting about University of Florida immediately after Drazen says he graduated there; Drazen replies 'Yes. But... they were they were pretty strict,' a natural rebuttal to a 'party school' quip. UF has that colloquial reputation.

blocks.clean_summary: Drazen continues about the University of Florida: students had to earn their AA and apply to an 'upper division' school or be kicked out; his was liberal arts and sciences. He wanted to live in New York City, was there by December 1984, graduated from law school, and then moved to Los Angeles (year garbled as 'fall of 198'). Faraaz notes UF is a very good school in medicine.

corrections.basis: Line 79: 'graduated from law school and and I moved to Los Angeles in the fall of 198.' Truncated digit. A standard three-year JD begun ~fall 1985 would end 1988, but the final digit is not in the text; flagged rather than fixed.

blocks.clean_summary: Geographic small talk: Drazen clarifies the University of Florida is in Gainesville, north-central Florida (not Miami), inland and brutally hot in summer. He then moved to New York, later Los Angeles (which he didn't love), then back east to Westchester, commuting into the city until about 1991-92, when he returned to Binghamton.

corrections.basis: Line 101: 'I I came back to Bingington' — same phonetic garble of Binghamton, Drazen's practice location.

blocks.clean_summary: Nostalgia about NYC student life. Drazen recalls his studio apartment with a brick-wall view renting for $692, guessing it would be about $2,000 now (Faraaz says $10,000 easily); his last apartment was about $700. Faraaz asks whether New York was always this hot, saying the heat is unbearable now.

Drazen describes his last apartment's small terrace with a view of the George Washington Bridge and praises the Upper West Side as a 24-hour part of the city, contrasting it with the East Side where everything closed at 11. Faraaz calls the East Side 'bougie' and 'prim and proper' (transcribed 'proven and proper'). Drazen says he preferred the West Side but his East Side spot was okay because it was next to a subway entrance for his commute to school near Union Square.

corrections.basis: Line 129, Faraaz characterizing the Upper East Side right after calling it 'bougie'; 'prim and proper' is the standard idiom and phonetically close.
